population.note: FICTIONAL. Cycling arithmetic: ever 32.0% − current 21.2% = 10.8% of adults have used and are off now. About 9.6 pts of current users are on a second or later course, and ≈3.8 pts of the off-now group restarted at least once and stopped again, so (9.6+3.8)/32.0 = 42% cycled, flat on 2030. Two things pull against each other here. $39–69 generics and the free health-centre programme make restarting almost frictionless. Monthly MariTide and longer coverage-independent cash courses raise persistence, to ≈42% at one year overall and ≈55% on monthly dosing. Of ~272M adults: ≈57.7M current, ≈29.4M used and off now, ≈185M never used. Ever-use rose 8.0 pts (≈21.8M new first-time users in the window), the biggest first-start wave since 2026, because price stopped being the barrier. Age check: 18–29 12.5% × 52M = 6.5M; 30–49 23.5% × 90M = 21.2M; 50–64 33% × 62M = 20.5M; 65+ 13.5% × 68M = 9.2M; total ≈ 57.4M ≈ 21.1%, consistent with 21.2% given rounding. 65+ rose 5 pts despite the bone wave because generic semaglutide in the Medicare Bridge costs beneficiaries $0–10 and many older users who paused in 2029–30 restarted. A DEXA-advised pause is still the largest single reason older users are off. Income: the bottom third rose from 10.3% to 18.0%, mostly through cash generics at $39–69, the HHS health-centre programme (≈2.6M) and Medicaid generic substitution. Imported or counterfeit use fell from ≈3.1M to ≈1.2M. The gap with the top third (24.0%) narrowed in level and widened in kind: top-third users are disproportionately on tirzepatide, retatrutide or monthly MariTide with scans, while bottom-third users are on generic weekly semaglutide, mostly without scans. The ≈185M never-users are increasingly people who refuse on principle, people under 30, and the uninsured rural poor who live far from a participating health centre. Price no longer explains much of this group. Pediatric: ≈0.9% of ~73M under-18s (≈660k), mostly adolescents 12+ on generic semaglutide. Interim adolescent bone-accrual data appeared in 2032 (see ledger). Roughly one US child in five now lives with an adult who is currently on the drug.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: from Jan 2032 the Bridge successor went generic-first. Generic semaglutide at ≈$45/month net, with a $0–10 copay. Brand tirzepatide, retatrutide or MariTide requires step therapy at $199 with the $50 copay. Medicare pays ≈17.5% of fills ≈ 10.1M users (9.2M aged 65+ plus ≈0.9M disabled under 65), of whom ≈3.6M use the Bridge for obesity: 2.6M × $45 × 12 = $1.4B plus 1.0M × $199 × 12 = $2.4B ≈ $3.8B in 2032, down from $4.3B in 2030 even though Bridge users doubled. Counselling-visit and fall-risk templates are retained. Medicaid pays ≈13% of fills ≈ 7.5M users: 5.5M generic × $35 × 12 = $2.3B plus 2.0M brand (diabetes/cardiac codes) × $199 × 12 = $4.8B ≈ $7.1B gross, before rebates. HHS National Incretin Access Program (Mar 2032): free generic semaglutide through Section 330 health centres for adults with obesity below 200% FPL who are uninsured or have no weight coverage. ≈2.6M enrolled by Dec 2032 (4.5% of fills): drug 2.6M × $32 × 12 ≈ $1.0B, plus visits and labs at ≈$300 per enrollee per year ≈ $0.8B, ≈ $1.8B a year, inside the $2.0B FY2032 appropriation. The DEXA voucher line is capped at ≈400k scans. The Indiana and Arkansas waivers are unchanged.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 100+ semaglutide brands at $3–20/month, plus first generic liraglutide-sema combinations. China: generic semaglutide is domestic and exported, and Chinese generic tirzepatide is sold domestically and in ASEAN, Latin America and the Gulf despite patent disputes. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 40–70. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and the EU (semaglutide generics since 2031 in most member states) have them too. Generic oral semaglutide is sold everywhere except the US.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Generic collapse for semaglutide only. Generic weekly injectable semaglutide launched Jan 2032 under Paragraph IV settlements, with ANDAs referencing Ozempic and Wegovy 2.4 mg. It launched at $99 and is $39–69/month cash at chain and warehouse pharmacies by Q4 2032. Novo's authorised generic sells at $59. Wegovy 7.2 mg, the Wegovy pill and Rybelsus remain branded. Tirzepatide is on patent to ~2036 and is $149–199 on the federal direct portal (launched as TrumpRx). Foundayo starting doses are still $149. Retatrutide: $1,499 list, $349 direct. MariTide (monthly, Amgen): $1,150 list, $349 direct, $299 with a clinic-administered bundle. Payer mix of ≈57.7M users: commercial 26% (15.0M, mostly diabetes, cardiovascular, OSA, CKD and MASH codes), Medicare 17.5% (10.1M), Medicaid 13% (7.5M), HHS programme 4.5% (2.6M), cash/direct 37% (21.3M, of which ≈15M generic semaglutide, ≈3.5M branded direct and ≈2.8M 'calm' and 'compulsion' subscriptions), imported/counterfeit 2% (1.2M) = 100%. The main question is now the income floor, not the price. $49 a month plus a $25–40 telehealth script and no DEXA is the default tier. The 503B exclusion and 503A injunction stand. Gray trade has moved to next-generation molecules, with Chinese 'reta' vials at $60–90 and no prescription.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable, branded and US generic (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, incl. 7.2 mg; generics from 8+ ANDA holders)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular agonist, weekly injectable (amycretin, approved Nov 2031)
GLP-1 agonist / GIPR antagonist antibody-peptide conjugate, monthly injectable (maridebart cafraglutide: MariTide, approved Jun 2031)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda and generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: smoking and vaping cessation (semaglutide 2.4 mg, Aug 2032; label includes anhedonia monitoring at weeks 4 and 12)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'calm', 'focus' and 'craving freedom' subscriptions, now mostly on generic low-dose injectable semaglutide or Foundayo at $49–129/month
gambling, compulsive shopping and 'doomscroll' compulsion, prescribed by telehealth ahead of the pending Foundayo sNDA
'metabolic health' / longevity regimens in concierge practices, now mostly MariTide
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
pornography and sexual-compulsion programmes run by some faith-based and secular recovery clinics, an anecdotal and contested use
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. MariTide (filed Apr 2030) was approved in Jun 2031, 14 months after filing. It is the monthly driver: a clinic- or self-administered monthly dose with ~16–20% loss, and the label requires baseline DEXA for users over 50. ≈2.4M Americans were on it by Dec 2032. No implant exists. Amycretin was approved in Nov 2031 with 72-week DEXA data in the label. Survodutide was resubmitted in Sep 2031 and got a second CRL in Mar 2032 over heart rate; it is not on the market. The semaglutide smoking-cessation resubmission (Jan 2032, on a 2029–31 trial with SHAPS endpoints) was approved in Aug 2032. The compulsion indication is realised as a filing, not an approval. Lilly filed an sNDA for Foundayo in gambling disorder in Apr 2032 on two phase 3 trials begun in 2029. It has priority review plus a 3-month extension for anhedonia data, and the action date is Apr 2033. Bimagrumab combinations are still in phase 3, unfiled. US semaglutide generics arrived via settlement in Jan 2032. Incretin market ≈$104B in 2032: US volume up ~45%, US semaglutide net revenue down ~60%, Lilly and Amgen growing, Novo contracting. Bone agents remain routine co-prescriptions in the insured tier.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of voluntary stopping. First-dose GI events on MariTide are front-loaded and heavier for some, and a monthly dose cannot be skipped once given. Unsupervised generic escalation causes more ED visits than branded use did.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; severe gastroparesis caution retained; MariTide label recommends titration via a lower first dose.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Rising in absolute numbers with ~58M users and wider retatrutide and amycretin use.
No causal confirmation; absolute risk low; counterfeit confounding is falling as imports shrink.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL litigation ongoing, with bellwether trials set for 2033.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A recognised population problem. Lean mass makes up ~30–40% of weight lost in users over 50 who do not resistance-train. Generic-tier users rarely get body-composition testing: in health-system data, <15% of cash generic users over 50 have had a DEXA, against ~70% in insured plans. Grip-strength decline is now measurable in 50–64 men as well as women.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label retained; MariTide and amycretin labels carry baseline DEXA language for over-50s; Medicare counselling visit includes a strength-referral template. Generic labels match the reference labels. Nobody funds the scans for the cash tier.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Second wave year. ≈4.5M users aged 65+ have more than 2 years' use: 0.6%/yr baseline hip-fracture rate × 0.35 excess × 4.5M ≈ 9,500 excess hip fractures a year, against ~300,000 total. The 50–64 cycler signal (HR ~1.2) is replicated in a VA cohort. Medicare DEXA claims are up ~75% on 2028, and waits in the Southeast and Mountain West run 10–14 weeks.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class labelling retained. In May 2032 FDA added a class 'Limitations of Use' paragraph recommending body-composition and BMD assessment before and during use beyond 2 years in adults 65+ and in postmenopausal women; it is not boxed. The DOJ civil case against Novo settled in 2031 for $1.1B with no admission.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention; no class determination.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association in the cessation trial's C-SSRS data or in updated reviews.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the grey')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Moved from emerging to established. The randomised smoking-cessation trial showed SHAPS anhedonia crossing threshold in ~7% on semaglutide 2.4 mg versus ~4% on placebo at 12 weeks, mostly resolving on dose reduction. The retatrutide observational top-dose figure stands at ~10–14%. Low-dose 'calm' users remain unmeasured.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled in the cessation indication with SHAPS screening at weeks 4 and 12; FDA requested anhedonia data for the Foundayo compulsion sNDA; FTC warning letters continue.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Substantial regain within a year. A new source of involuntary stops is employer retreat in 2031–32, which drops covered users mid-course. Most switch to generic semaglutide, but tirzepatide and retatrutide users who switch to semaglutide regain partially (~3–6% of body weight).
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly. Indiana waiver litigation is still pending in the Seventh Circuit.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Signals are strongest in high-loss, older and low-income users. Health centres report iron and B12 deficiency in HHS-programme enrollees whose diets were already constrained.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance (protein ≥1.2 g/kg, vitamin D and calcium); HHS programme includes a baseline lab panel; no FDA action.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~9 years; adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About ten years of follow-up. In 2032 interim adolescent bone-accrual data reported lumbar BMD accrual ~0.2 SD lower at 2 years than in matched controls. It is unreplicated and confounded by weight loss itself. Cycling still looks worse for bone than continuous use.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric PMRs continue; AAP issued an interim statement recommending DEXA at baseline and 24 months for adolescents; no label change.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Falling for semaglutide as legal generics undercut imports. Poison-centre calls involving mail-order product are down ~40% from the 2030 peak. Harm has moved to gray 'reta' and 'cagri' vials sold to people without prescriptions, including some under 21.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alerts extended to retatrutide-labelled API; no individual prosecutions; no new importation law.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A few percent; transient; also reported with gray-market vials.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Moved from emerging to established. Two claims cohorts that adjust for frailty indices find ~1.2× fall-related ED visits in 65+ users with more than 2 years' use, mediated by sarcopenia and orthostatic symptoms.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Fall-risk screening is in the Bridge counselling template and the 2032 class Limitations of Use.

safety_ledger.effect: Monthly-depot inflexibility (MariTide): inability to hold or reduce a dose quickly during adverse effects or anhedonia
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New. Users who develop GI intolerance or 'the grey' cannot take a weekend holiday; effects persist for weeks. Some PBM and clinic programmes favour monthly dosing because adherence is automatic, which removes the user's own dose control.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Label advises a lower initiation dose; no REMS; FDA postmarketing study on discontinuation kinetics.

food_and_beverage.state: Volume losses now reach the households that were heaviest on snacks. With bottom-third uptake at 18%, dollar-store and convenience salty-snack and sugary-drink volume is down ~4–5% a year in 2031–32, against ~2–3% in premium grocery earlier. Packaged-food majors are selling or merging mid-tier snack brands and moving into protein, fibre and 'bone-forward' fortified lines. The 'real food, full portion' heritage brands are a durable niche. In Mississippi and Alabama, school districts are cutting à-la-carte snack contracts as vendors withdraw.

alcohol.state: Fourth and fifth years of US spirits volume decline. Beer is down ~2% a year. 'Calm' and 'compulsion' prescribing takes occasional drinkers. Cigarette and vape volumes fall faster after the August cessation approval, and tobacco majors guide to an extra 1–2 pts of annual decline. Non-alcoholic and 'one good drink' formats hold.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat; spend per cover is down nationally, no longer only in suburbs. Value chains in the South and Midwest are closing units as their core customers come onto generics. Gram-priced bowls and half-portion menus are standard. The 'no-gram' independents in Atlanta, Memphis and Houston are still full and now franchise.

apparel.state: Size churn continues, driven now by employer-coverage switches and tier changes as much as by cycling. Discount chains carry wider size runs on shorter cycles. Plus-size specialists hold their share by marketing to the off-by-conviction audience.

fitness.state: Growing, but along a class line. DEXA-plus-coaching chains and Medicare Advantage strength benefits serve the insured tier, while health-centre 'bands and bodyweight' classes and church-basement strength groups serve the generic tier. DEXA capacity is the binding constraint in the Southeast.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage fell from 63% to 41%. Employers argued that $49 generics made the benefit unnecessary, and bone claims, gating litigation and EEOC charges made it costly. Diabetes, CV, OSA, CKD and MASH codes are still covered almost universally, so coding has become a battleground: claims carrying 'prediabetes' and OSA diagnoses are up sharply. PBMs offer 'generic cash card' referrals in place of coverage. Pharmacy trend has eased to ~+3%.

pharma.state: Lilly leads on tirzepatide, retatrutide and Foundayo. Novo is contracting: its US semaglutide revenue is collapsing to generics, and it is leaning on amycretin, CagriSema and the authorised generic. Amgen's MariTide is the fastest-growing brand, through clinic bundles and longevity practices. Generic makers (Teva, Viatris, Dr. Reddy's, Sandoz and others) run on thin margins with high volume. Bone-agent and DEXA suppliers are still growing.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on the drug no longer signals class; what you are on does. 'Generic sema' is the standard weekly pen in a pharmacy bag. A MariTide clinic visit or resistance-trained shoulders signal the insured or affluent tier. The 'on it too long' stoop is now joked about in people over 60. 'Off' still has its medical and principled readings, and a third has become common: 'they dropped my coverage and I switched to generic'.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The level gap narrowed (24% top third vs 18% bottom) and the quality gap hardened. The top gets retatrutide or monthly MariTide with scans, coaching and antiresorptives. The bottom gets $49 generic semaglutide by telehealth, or free from a health centre with a 10–14-week DEXA wait. In Jackson, Mississippi, the free-pen programme at the health centres drew queues on launch day, and local pharmacists say generic semaglutide now outsells insulin by box count.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Protein-first, smaller shared meals are the norm. Heritage defences such as Sunday dinners, church potlucks and the 'no-gram' rooms are now an organised counter-culture with cookbooks and festivals. School cafeterias in the Deep South face a new issue: older students on generic semaglutide skip lunch.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Profiles list on/off and increasingly the molecule. 'Unmedicated' remains a filter. 'Monthly' is a dating disclosure: it means you can't drop a dose for a weekend.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is still medicalised, and since the cessation approval craving in general is too: nicotine today, gambling pending. The backlash coalition has split over the free programme. The Atlanta body-sovereignty collectives call it 'treatment offered to Black and poor bodies instead of food, time and money' but defend recipients from shaming. The Tulsa–Dallas congregations preach against 'pharmaceutical contentment' and are now joined by some Black Baptist pulpits in Jackson and Birmingham. Supplement influencers sell 'detox from the pen' protocols. Disability advocates support the free programme because it is ungated.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. The first randomised figures from the cessation trial (~7% vs ~4% placebo at 2.4 mg) make 'the grey' a labelled, measured effect at standard dose, and retatrutide top-dose observational figures (~10–14%) still frame the upper bound. With ≈57.7M users, even a 3-point excess at standard doses implies on the order of 1.5–2M people with measurable flattening. About 2.8M people pay for 'calm' or 'compulsion' subscriptions; nobody measures them systematically, though two academic surveys suggest high satisfaction alongside self-reported lower enjoyment of music and sex.
interior_life.framing: A side effect everyone knows about and manages. 'The grey' is ordinary speech, as in 'I'm a bit grey this week, I've dropped to 0.5'. Pharmacists counsel dose holidays on weekly generics. Wellness brands have softened their copy from 'calm' to 'steadier', partly after FTC letters. Clinicians now say 'reward dampening' to patients and SHAPS to each other.
interior_life.effect_on_work: With employer coverage retreating, employers have less visibility. Fewer PBM dashboards exist, and the remaining gating covers mostly diabetes-code users. Tech and finance firms still reimburse 'focus' subscriptions through lifestyle accounts. Fleets, warehouses and call centres say nothing officially, and some managers quietly prefer the steadier staff. Workers in sales, kitchens, bars, stages and pulpits routinely cut their dose before high-stakes days. Unions have started bargaining over whether a monthly-depot clinic programme can be offered as a benefit 'in lieu of' cash.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Written off-dose' is still a selling point in Nashville and in stand-up. A new genre of 'grey' ambient and lo-fi music is made by and for users and sells to them. Casino operators in Las Vegas and Atlantic City and the sportsbook apps report softer handle among younger bettors and are lobbying against the Foundayo gambling filing through 'responsible gaming' groups that oppose 'medicalising fun'.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Weekend dose holidays are normal on weekly products and impossible on monthly ones. Couples counsellors report 'molecule mismatch' when one partner moves to MariTide. Sex therapists screen routinely. Backlash churches run 'whole-hearted marriage' retreats for couples coming off.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Mostly about who pays and what is free. Republicans are split between taking credit for the portal prices and opposing an HHS giveaway. Democrats push to expand the health-centre programme and are wary of the bone data. The 'calm voter' question is out in public: a 2032 political-science preprint finds no turnout difference among users once age and income are controlled, but campaign consultants still segment for it. The cessation approval let some states fold generic semaglutide into tobacco-quitline benefits.

state.regulatory_posture: FDA is data-demanding but approving: MariTide and amycretin with DEXA labelling, semaglutide cessation with SHAPS monitoring, a second CRL for survodutide, and an anhedonia-data extension for the compulsion sNDA. Generic approvals were fast once the settlements opened the market. Import enforcement has shifted to retatrutide and other gray-market API. The FTC still polices advertising claims only.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Subsidy, not mandate. The HHS National Incretin Access Program gives free generic semaglutide through Section 330 health centres to adults below 200% FPL with obesity and no weight coverage: ≈2.6M enrolled, ≈$1.8B a year (arithmetic in access.public_coverage), and no gating beyond a 6-monthly visit. Medicare's generic-first Bridge costs beneficiaries $0–10. Eleven states fund generic semaglutide through tobacco quitlines after the cessation approval. Nothing is required of anyone.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Public conditioning is unchanged: the Indiana and Arkansas waivers still require ≥80% PDC and quarterly weigh-ins. Private conditioning has shrunk with employer retreat, since fewer employers cover and so fewer gate. BMI-linked wellness surcharges up to 30% of premium remain legal and in use. The new data stream is pharmacy loyalty and telehealth subscription data on cash generic buyers, which is outside HIPAA and is sold to marketers.
state.workforce_or_military: DOT sleep-apnea screening still pushes drivers toward tirzepatide, now mostly covered under OSA codes. Some fleets offer free generic semaglutide on site. The Army opened a pilot in 2031 allowing accession for recruits stable on generic semaglutide for 12 months with a DEXA; it is contested by some commanders. Fleets keep DEXA screening for drivers over 55.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Legal US generics are made largely in India, with Chinese API in some ANDAs, which revives Section 232 and 'pharma security' arguments in Congress. Generic makers got domestic-fill tariff credits. Chinese generic tirzepatide is sold across Latin America and Asia under patent challenge, and Lilly and the USTR treat it as a trade issue. The India–US trade talks have dropped mail-order pharma as a bargaining item because it matters less now.

events.event: FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-monthly obesity injection, with baseline DEXA language for patients over 50; Amgen prices it at $349 a month direct and bundles clinic-administered doses for longevity practices and Medicare Advantage plans

Mercer and KFF surveys show large employers dropping weight-management GLP-1 coverage for 2032 plan years while keeping diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnea codes; Walmart-scale retailers and two state employee plans exit, citing imminent $50 generics, fracture claims and EEOC charges over gating

Generic injectable semaglutide launches in the US under Paragraph IV settlements with eight ANDA holders and a Novo authorised generic; launch cash price of $99 falls to $39–69 at chain and warehouse pharmacies by autumn

HHS launches the National Incretin Access Program, free generic semaglutide through community health centres for low-income adults with obesity and no weight coverage, funded at $2.0B; health centres in Jackson, Memphis and the Rio Grande Valley report waitlists within weeks

FDA adds a class 'Limitations of Use' recommending bone and body-composition assessment beyond two years for adults over 65 and postmenopausal women, as a VA cohort replicates the cycling-fracture signal; at a Birmingham rally, Atlanta body-sovereignty collectives and Southern pulpits split publicly over whether the free-pen programme is care or 'pacification'

FDA approves semaglutide for smoking and vaping cessation with SHAPS anhedonia screening in the label, the first time 'the grey' appears as a measured labelled effect; Lilly's April sNDA for Foundayo in gambling disorder is on priority review with an action date extended to April 2033

open_tensions: Two tiers have hardened. Insured patients with qualifying diagnosis codes get tirzepatide, retatrutide or monthly MariTide with scans and coaching, while everyone else gets $49 generic semaglutide or a free health-centre pen with no body-composition monitoring. The bone guidance now says scans are needed, and no one funds them for the larger tier. DEXA capacity in the Southeast is 10–14 weeks out.

Monthly dosing solves adherence by removing the user's control over dose. Payers and clinic programmes favour it at the same moment that 'the grey' has become a labelled effect whose standard remedy is a dose holiday.

The Foundayo gambling-disorder decision in April 2033 would put craving reduction formally on label beyond food and nicotine. Casinos, sportsbooks, the religious backlash and the FTC's record on 'calm' marketing are all lining up, and roughly 2.8M people already buy the effect off-label.

The free federal programme and Medicare's generic-first Bridge are cheap enough to expand, which splits the backlash coalition: disability advocates defend ungated free access, while body-sovereignty and religious groups call it medicating poverty. Neither party has a stable position going into 2033 budget fights.
still_true: Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it; generic semaglutide made it irrelevant.
Retatrutide's list price is still $1,499 a month.

The Indiana and Arkansas Medicaid 1115 waivers still require ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered and quarterly verified weigh-ins; two misses end coverage for 12 months, and the Seventh Circuit disability-rights litigation is still unresolved.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.
The 503B exclusion and the 503A injunction on compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide still stand, and Congress has passed no new importation law.

prose.headline: Forty-Nine Dollars, No Scan: Generic Semaglutide Made America's Weight Drug Cheap. Now Who Checks Your Bones?
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2032 a little over one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, and for the first time price explains very little about who is and who isn't. In January the first US generics of injectable semaglutide reached pharmacy shelves under patent settlements negotiated years earlier. They launched at ninety-nine dollars a month and by autumn sold for thirty-nine to sixty-nine at warehouse clubs and chain pharmacies. Novo sells its own authorised generic at fifty-nine. Wegovy still has a list price of $1,349, a number that now exists mainly on paper.

Cheap made coverage look optional, and employers acted on that. Through 2031 large retailers, two state employee plans and hundreds of mid-sized firms dropped weight-management coverage for the 2032 plan year. Their reasons were that workers could now afford it themselves, that fracture claims were arriving, and that gating had brought discrimination charges. Coverage fell from nearly two-thirds of employers to about two in five. Diabetes, heart, sleep-apnea and kidney codes are still covered almost everywhere, so a diagnosis now decides which tier you are in. With one you get tirzepatide, retatrutide or Amgen's new monthly injection, MariTide, with a body scan and a coach. Without one you get a weekly generic pen, a forty-dollar telehealth visit and nothing else.

Washington took the other path. In March HHS began giving generic semaglutide away free through community health centres to low-income adults with obesity and no coverage. About 2.6 million people enrolled within nine months at a cost of roughly $1.8 billion a year, cheaper than the Medicare programme it sits beside. Medicare went generic-first in January, and its beneficiaries now pay between nothing and ten dollars. Uptake among the poorest third of adults has nearly doubled in two years. The clinics in Jackson, Memphis and the Rio Grande Valley have waitlists. Waits for a DEXA scan are longer still.

The bone story has not gone away; it has spread to more people. Around nine and a half thousand extra hip fractures a year are now attributed to long-term use in older Americans, and a third cohort has confirmed that women who cycle on and off fare worse. In May the FDA added language to every label recommending bone and body-composition checks after two years. In insured plans most people over fifty have had one. Among people paying cash for generics, fewer than one in six have. The guidance has reached everyone, and the funding for scans reaches only the insured.

The drugs' quieting effect is no longer contested, only managed. In August the FDA approved semaglutide for quitting cigarettes and vapes, and the trial behind it gave the effect a number: about seven percent of users at the standard dose lost a measurable amount of pleasure, against four percent on placebo. Users still call it 'the grey' and treat it as routine. Pharmacists advise skipping a weekly dose before a wedding. People on the monthly shot cannot do that, and they say so. Lilly has asked for approval to treat gambling disorder, with a decision due in April, and the casinos have begun lobbying against what they call 'medicalising fun'.

The backlash that marched together in Atlanta two years ago has split over free pens. Body-sovereignty collectives say the poor are being offered injections instead of groceries and time. Southern pulpits, now including some Black Baptist churches, preach against 'pharmaceutical contentment'. Disability advocates defend the programme because nobody has to step on a scale to stay in it. Snack volumes at dollar stores are falling faster than they ever did at Whole Foods, spirits are in a fifth year of decline, and tobacco companies have cut their guidance. From a distance the country looks steadier and calmer, and it is noticeably quieter.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Harlan, fifty-four, manages the cafeteria at Callaway High in Jackson. She is at the steam line by six-forty, counting trays. The district cut the chip vendor in January, and the empty rack still stands by the register like a tooth gap.

The state plan dropped her Zepbound last fall. Her A1c is 5.9, one tenth short of the code that would have kept it. Now it's the generic, a box of four pens for fifty-four dollars at the Walmart on County Line Road, plus thirty-five a quarter to a telehealth nurse in Ohio she has never seen in person. She lost six pounds back in the switch, then held steady.

At lunch a junior named Marcus takes a tray and leaves it full. 'You on it?' she asks. He shrugs, which means yes. She slides him a milk. Protein, the poster says.

At three-thirty she calls the health centre about a bone scan. The first opening is February 11th. The woman on the phone says the free programme is for people under two hundred percent of poverty, and Denise is over by four thousand dollars.

At Wednesday service Pastor Oliver preaches on manna, how God gave enough and no more and the people were not to store it. A woman in the row ahead has her own pen in her handbag, the orange cap showing.

That night Denise skips her dose, because Saturday is her niece's wedding and she wants to cry at it. She sets a phone reminder for Sunday. She stands in the kitchen and eats a slice of pound cake, slowly, and it tastes like something.
